content: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used to treat a variety of bacterial infections. It may also be prescribed to prevent certain bacterial infections. This medication is effective only against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections such as the common cold or flu. Take erythromycin by mouth as directed by your doctor, with or without food. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. For optimal results, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. If you are using it to treat an infection, continue taking it for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication too early may result in a return of the infection. If you are taking it to prevent an infection, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Common side effects of erythromycin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain or cramping, and loss of appetite. Taking the medication with food may help reduce these symptoms. Remember that your doctor has prescribed this medication because they believe the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, erythromycin may cause a severe intestinal condition due to a bacteria called Clostridium difficile (C. diff). This condition can occur during treatment or weeks to months after stopping the medication. Prolonged or repeated use of erythromycin may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare but possible. Before taking erythromycin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other macrolide antibiotics (such as azithromycin or clarithromycin), or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other problems. Erythromycin may also cause a condition affecting the heart rhythm known as QT prolongation, which can increase the risk of serious irregular heartbeats. The risk of QT prolongation may be higher if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can also increase this risk, especially if caused by severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Erythromycin may interfere with live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine, making them less effective. Some erythromycin products may contain sodium, which could be relevant for individuals on a sodium-restricted diet. Additionally, this medication passes into breast milk, so consult your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Infants may be at a higher risk of developing a serious stomach condition when exposed to erythromycin. Drug interactions can alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Other medications may affect the removal of erythromycin from your body, potentially altering its effectiveness. Similarly, erythromycin can slow the removal of other drugs from your body, which may affect how they work. This medication may also interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as urine tests, potentially causing false results. If someone overdoses on erythromycin and experiences severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. In the U.S., you can call 1-800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Different brands of erythromycin may have different storage requirements. Check the product packaging for specific instructions or ask your pharmacist. Do not freeze the medication or store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about erythromycin. It does not guarantee that the medication is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
